entries.note: From the photos: inscription on the front free endpaper thanks Giblin for kind help, signed at the foot with Porter's address at Temple Fortune Lane, London NW11. Pencilled '#95 Signed copy' in the top corner, apparently a later cataloguing note. Map of Tasmania printed on the front pastedown. Frontispiece photo captioned The Approach to Launceston. Cloth frayed at the spine ends. Jacket is the right one for the book and keeps its 18/- price, but has chips, tears with loss, old tape stains on the rear panel corners and a split spine panel with loss at the head. Rear panel blurb (only partly legible) says Porter had spent his working life looking after other people's money, seemingly as a bank manager, and had friends in Tasmania. Buyer's premium rate not seen.

entries.title: R.W. Giblin identified: Ronald Worthy Giblin (1863-1936), surveyor and historian of early Tasmania
entries.note: Ronald Worthy Giblin (born Hobart 3 Jan 1863, died London 13 Mar 1936), surveyor and historian. Per the Australian Dictionary of Biography (vol. 8, 1981, article by Ian Pearce, https://adb.anu.edu.au/biography/giblin-ronald-worthy-6304): Tasmanian Lands Department from 1884, licensed surveyor in NSW 1889, joined the Royal Survey Department of Siam in 1894 and directed it 1901 to 1910 (Order of the White Elephant), then settled in England at Cheltenham. From 1916 he was indent officer in the London office of Tasmania's Agent-General. The Tasmanian government commissioned him in 1921 to research the early settlement years and he resigned in 1924 to write full time. Volume 1 of The Early History of Tasmania (The Geographical Era 1642 to 1804, Methuen, London, 1928) came out with a 300 pound Tasmanian government grant, and the ADB calls it 'the definitive work on this subject'. His unfinished volume 2 was edited by Archer (J.D.A.) Collier of the Tasmanian Public Library and published in 1939. Wikipedia and the UTAS Special and Rare Collections record (https://heritage.utas.edu.au/index.php/ronald-worthy-giblin) say he was a Fellow of the Royal Geographical Society and of the Royal Colonial Institute; UTAS adds he joined the Royal Society of Tasmania in 1926, published in its Papers and Proceedings in 1925 and 1929, and was a grandson of Robert Wilkins Giblin of the prominent Hobart Giblin family. The Companion to Tasmanian History entry (Wendy Rimon) agrees on the main facts. Why collectors care: he is the standard historian of Tasmania before 1804 and a recognised Hobart name, though not a big-money one. The inscribee fits him on every point (name, FRGS, living in London in 1934 as Porter was, Tasmanian subject) and I found no other Ronald W. Giblin FRGS. Whether Porter's preface, text or index names him is not established: no online text of the book or of its 1935 Geographical Journal review was reachable. The inscription's thanks for kind help suggests he assisted with the book, but that is inference from the inscription only.

value_estimate_aud: Probably worth A$60 to A$150 at auction, and I would not go much past A$120 to A$150 all-in including buyer's premium. Evidence is thin, so this is judgement. A plain copy is cheap: the only two copies on AbeBooks today ask US$20.80 (UK, fair, no jacket) and US$32.12 (Berkelouw NSW, jacket not mentioned), roughly A$30 to A$50 at recent exchange rates before postage, and I found no auction results for the title at all. This copy adds three things: the original pictorial jacket (unclipped but tatty, which cuts its value a lot), a signed presentation inscription with the author's address, and a recipient who is the standard historian of early Tasmania, thanked for help with the book. That makes it a genuine association copy with a story a Tasmaniana collector will like, and the Launceston frontispiece suits a local shelf. But neither name carries big money: Giblin's own 1928 first edition lists at only US$20 to US$90 right now, and association premiums multiply a base value that is small here. A specialist dealer might ask something like A$150 to A$250 with a proper write-up, but I found no dealer comparable to prove that. At the current A$30 bid you are still paying plain-copy money, so the association is free so far. Above about A$200 you would be paying full retail for a book with a rough jacket. It would justify more if the preface or text thanks Giblin by name, or if the book carries his bookplate or signature.
still_to_check: 1. At viewing, or by asking the auctioneer for photos, check the preface, any acknowledgements and the index for Giblin's name, and look for a Giblin bookplate or ownership signature on the endpapers. 2. Check the plates and map against the list of illustrations (the number on the title page and jacket spine was not legible in the photos). 3. Buyer's premium rate for this sale. 4. Sold records in subscription or archive sources not reached within budget: Rare Book Hub, Australian Book Auctions, Gowans, Leski and Lawsons price archives, and eBay sold listings (blocked). 5. Dealer stock at Douglas Stewart, Hordern House, Peter Arnold, Antipodean Books and Astrolabe could not be searched (sites blocked or search not reachable). 6. Trove: 1934 to 1935 reviews in the Mercury or Examiner, which might say who Porter was and who helped him. 7. The 1935 Geographical Journal review on JSTOR (doi 10.2307/1787066). 8. Optional, for the story: Giblin's papers (ADB cites them at the Archives Office of Tasmania, now Libraries Tasmania) might hold letters from Porter.
